L1@P0: A Direct Construction of Non-Transitive Dice
L2@P0: Sets
L3@P0: Levi Angel and Matt Davis∗
L4@P0: Muskingum University
L5@P0: October 28, 2016
L6@P0: Abstract
L7@P0: In this paper, we give a direct construction for a set of dice realizing any
L8@P0: given tournament T . The construction for a tournament with n vertices
L9@P0: requires a number of sides on the order of n, which is the best general
L10@P0: construction to date. Our construction relies only on a standard theorem
L11@P0: from graph theory.
L12@P0: 1 Introduction
L13@P0: Non-transitive dice have been a object of wide interest since Martin Gardner
L14@P0: introduced some work (now known as Efron Dice) of Bradley Efron to the
L15@P0: general public in [5]. For a set of at least 3 dice {X1, X2, X3, . . .}, with faces
L16@P0: labeled in a nonstandard way, we define the relation  by declaring that Xi  Xj
L17@P0: exactly if, when the dice are rolled, the probability that Xi rolls a higher number
L18@P0: than Xj is greater than 1/2. Paradoxically, it is entirely possible to put numbers
L19@P0: on the dice in order to make the relation  non-transitive. The most basic
L20@P0: example of such a set of dice is the following set of three 3-sided dice:
L21@P0: Die: Faces:
L22@P0: X1 1,5,9
L23@P0: X2 3,4,8
L24@P0: X3 2,6,7
L25@P0: (1)
L26@P0: One can easily check that X1  X2, X2  X3, and X3  X1, where the
L27@P0: stronger die in each pair has probability 5/9 of winning. Note that we could
L28@P0: widen our focus and examine non-transitive sets of general random variables.
L29@P0: (See for example [8] and [9], which seem to predate any notion of non-transitive
L30@P0: dice specifically). However, even focusing on dice, there are many open questions.
